Posted on July 31, 2026 Bottom line up front: this long blog post describes the culmination of a years-long effort that means that we can now, modulo compiler bugs and a few unimportant edge cases, compile any Futhark program to parallel GPU code. Introduction One of the most interesting implementation challenges in Futhark is how to map nested parallelism, in which parallel operations can contain other parallel operations, to flat parallelism. This challenge arises because much interesting hardware (such as GPUs) does not efficiently support nested parallelism, and even on CPUs, arbitrary nesting may have significant run-time costs. Futhark has for a long time supported flattening only a limited (although important) subset of programs, called regular nested parallelism (as opposed to irregular), which meant that there were programs that we were unable to compile to GPU code. In 2022 I began an experimental implementation of “full flattening”, which as of this writing is the longest open pull request on the Futhark repository. I got far enough to build a proof of concept, but the sheer amount of effort involved led to the work stagnating - until now. Largely due to the efforts of students, we are now close to having a complete reimplementation of flattening in Futhark. The main contributions have been by Cornelius Sevald-Krause who implemented function and match lifting in his BSc thesis, and particularly by Amirreza Hashemi whose MSc work has been a whirlwind of finishing everything else. This includes various crucial optimisations in order to reach functionality and performance parity with the old flattener. I cannot overstate how impressive it is to come up with a systematic and maintainable replacement for a ten-year-old compiler pass that is full of optimisation heuristics. This post will introduce the basic problem of flattening, go through some of the various challenges, and explain how we have resolved them in the soon-to-be-merged work on the Futhark compiler. Flattening has a long academic pedigree, and I will try to link relevant other work, but this post is not a systematic survey of prior work. I will ignore most of the nontrivial bookkeeping that a compiler needs to do to actually implement all of this stuff, and instead focus on the intuition of how programs are transformed. I should mention up front what the goal is of this work: the new flattening transformation should not reduce performance for programs that already worked with the old implementation, but we are less concerned with the performance of programs that did not work before. As we shall see, achieving truly good performance on arbitrarily irregular nested parallelism is a major research problem in itself, and one that we intend to address incrementally in the time to come. Also, this is a long post. I have tried to make everything here relatively high-level, but you may want to skip to the reflections at the bottom if things drag on too much for your taste. Basics of flattening To motivate flattening, we’ll be assuming a slightly caricatured view of what a GPU can do. Expanding to full GPU functionality does not fundamentally change the story; it just means I would need more convoluted examples. Also, despite this post focusing on GPUs, you can mentally substitute “efficient but restricted processors” instead - these concerns crop up with any kind of vector processing. In the language of functional programming, we’ll start by assuming that a GPU can efficiently execute a map where the function contains sequential code, and where all memory for intermediate results can be allocated in advance. To avoid writing zip/unzip all the time, we’ll also suppose that our maps accept any number of arrays. This, for example, is something we can efficiently execute on a GPU: map (\x y -> x + y) xs ys (Incidentally, when describing the transformations to follow, it would be much simpler if map accepted its arrays before the lambda, like we do in Futhark’s IR - but I didn’t want to go that far in a blog post.) It is easy to imagine that this can be turned into a GPU program with one thread per iteration of the map. Apart from a single map with sequential code, we’ll also allow any nesting of maps. So this is also efficient: map (\xs ys -> map (\x y -> x + y) xs ys) xss yss It is similarly easy to imagine that these maps can be collapsed, with one GPU thread for every iteration of the innermost map. In addition to arbitrary sequential code, we will also allow the innermost operation to be a single parallel operation, such as a scan, a reduction, a transpose - the precise collection doesn’t really matter. Then this is also efficient: map (\xs -> reduce (+) 0 xs) xs Essentially, “efficient GPU code” means a tower of maps on top of some single parallel primitive operation (or sequential code). The reason these patterns are efficient is because we know how to generate efficient GPU kernels from these patterns. This has some relation to skeletons, but we don’t generally use that term, since we intend to use these patterns as a reasoning mechanism for the compiler, rather than a user-visible programming model. In the actual compiler, we of course have dedicated constructs to reliably express “a map with something specific inside of it”, but to minimise the syntax in this post, I will mostly stick with the towers-of-maps. Of course, Futhark programmers might not write programs that look like that. Such bold and free-thinking people might instead write this: map (\xs -> let y = reduce (+) 0 xs let zs = map (+y) xs in zs) xss This does fit one of the patterns we discussed: if we discard the parallelism of the inner map and reduce, then this is a map containing sequential code. This is an important choice when compiling a parallel language: you don’t have to exploit all the parallelism. Semantically, most parallel languages don’t require parallel execution in order to be correct; it’s just an option the implementation can take. Of course, we should not go overboard - a parallel language that does not exploit any parallelism might well be accused of violating the contract. In this case, we can rewrite the program to be one that is semantically identical, but is expressed in terms of the efficient patterns. To make it clear what is going on, first let us add some type annotations, where we assume that the shape of xs is [n][m]: map (\xs -> let y : i32 = reduce (+) 0 xs let zs : [m]i32 = map (+y) xs in zs) xss Then we split apart the outer map into two separate maps, with the first one returning an array of intermediate results that are passed into the second map: let ys = map (\xs -> reduce (+) 0 xs) xss let zss = map (\xs y -> map (+y) xs) xss ys These two maps now match the patterns that we know how to turn into efficient GPU code. The transformation we did here is often called loop distribution or fission, and is the counterpart to loop fusion. For a purely functional language, the following equation holds: map f ∘ map g = map (f∘g) (The rule is more convoluted once multiple input arrays are allowed, but let us ignore that.) Usually we apply the rule left-to-right in order to perform fusion and avoid having to store intermediate arrays in memory, but we can also apply it right-to-left, in which case it provides us a way to decompose complex maps into sequences of trivial maps that just perform one single operation (or a compound one - we can apply fission to the degree we want, which I will return to). This is the main technique we use for cutting apart an arbitrarily complex data parallel program into smaller manageable chunks. As far as I know, it was pioneered by Guy Blelloch in the early 90s as part of his work on NESL, although it was (and is) sometimes called “vectorization”, because its output, when fully applied, consists of maps and scans with trivial operations inside, which can be seen as “vector operations”. However, there are still two major problems we need to address before we have all the components of a working flattening algorithm. Irregular intermediate arrays Consider this program: map (\m -> let xs : [m]i64 = iota m let y : i64 = reduce (+) 0 xs in y) ns Recall that iota m produces an array [0, ..., m-1] of size m. This program has the same issue as above, in that the parallel operations are not perfectly nested. So let us try to fission (fise?) the map: let xss : [n][???]i64 = map (
 -> iota n) ns let ys = map (\xs -> reduce (+) 0 xs) xss Notice the question marks in the type of the xss binding - what size should we put there? Intuitively, the operation map (
 -> iota n) ns produces an irregular array, where the rows have different sizes, depending on the values of the input array ns. One might expect that map (
 -> iota n) [1,2,3] produces the array [[0],[0,1],[0,1,2]], but unfortunately, Futhark does not allow irregular arrays; neither in the source language nor in our IR. The reasons are motivated by performance, as once you have irregular arrays, you either need to represent arrays as arrays-of-pointers, or lose random access indexing. Neither are palatable when you want to target vector processors. That means we don’t want to allow irregular arrays in the source language, nor in the IR. This issue is the root of the limitation on our original flattening transformation, which is that it cannot handle irregular nested parallelism, meaning parallelism of a size that varies between iterations of outer parallel dimensions. In the example above, m is local to the outermost map, so the iota and reduce (both of which have a parallel width of m) are irregular. Our only choice would then be to sequentialise this code. Now, in the actual compiler, the iota would be fused into the reduce (using a representation I will not go into), but if we ignore that part, it seems like we are violating one of our constraints, which is that all memory for intermediate results must be preallocated - and here we need an array of size m, where m can be different for each thread. In this case, the problem can be solved by an inspector that extracts a slice of the program that computes all intermediate sizes (but not any other values), which is then used to compute memory requirements and organise intermediate results in memory. This can be done sometimes (roughly, when there is no tricky business with sequential loops), but it is a best-effort kind of thing, and it does not bring back parallelism. Anyway, the ability to handle irregular arrays is clearly crucial to the general goal of handling irregular nested parallelism. The solution is to figure out a representation of irregular arrays as flat (one-dimensional arrays), which still allow the parallel execution of the operations we need. The central building block is an encoding of a two-dimensional irregular array as a data vector and a flag vector, both of the same size. The data vector is merely the rows of the array concatenated, while the flag vector indicates whether its corresponding element is the beginning of a new row. Example: Nested irregular array: [[1], [2,3], [4,5,6]] Value vector: [1,2,3,4,5,6] Flag vector: [true, true, false, true, false, false] (The restriction to two-dimensional arrays is without loss of generality: we can always collapse extra inner dimensions and have auxiliary arrays telling us how to reconstruct them. For simplicity, we will not go into further detail.) We call this a segmented array, and the “irregular rows” are called segments. The array above has three segments, of size 1, 2, and 3 respectively. In practice, we often use certain additional auxiliary arrays, for tracking the size of each segment (the shape vector, in this example [1,2,3]), the beginning offset of each segment in the data vector (the offset vector, [0,1,3] here), and arrays associating each element of the data array to its segment index ([0,1,1,2,2,2]) and in-segment index ([0,0,1,0,1,2]). These can all be efficiently computed from the flag vector, however. The fundamental operation on this representation is the segmented scan, which can be defined in terms of the standard scan as follows: def segscan 't [n] (op: t -> t -> t) (ne: t) (flags: [n]bool) (vals: [n]t) : [n]t = let pairs = scan (\(v1, f1) (v2, f2) -> let f = f1 || f2 let v = if f2 then v2 else op v1 v2 in (v, f)) (ne, false) (zip vals flags) let (res, _) = unzip pairs in res We can apply it to the representation of the irregular array above to obtain the result of (inclusively) scanning each segment, concatenated into a single array: > segscan (+) 0 [true, true, false, true, false, false] [1,2,3,4,5,6] [1, 2, 5, 4, 9, 15] This is the value array for a segmented array representing [1,2,5]++[4,9]++[15], using the original flag array unchanged. Since scans are such an important building block in parallel algorithms, it is no surprise that once we can scan these segmented arrays, we can do all kinds of other things as well. For example, we can do a segmented reduction by first performing a segmented scan, then extracting the final element of each scanned segment: def segreduce 't [n] (op: t -> t -> t) (ne: t) (flags: [n]bool) (vals: [n]t) : ?[m].[m]t = segscan op ne flags vals |> zip (rotate 1 flags) |> filter (.0) |> map (.1) > segreduce (+) 0 [true, true, false, true, false, false] [1,2,3,4,5,6] [1, 5, 15] Similarly, we can construct a segmented iota, which takes as input a shape vector of type []i64, and morally maps iota over this array. The construction is based on the observation that a normal iota can be written as an exclusive prefix sum over an array comprising n copies of 1: def iota n = expresum (replicate n 1) A segmented iota is then just a segmented scan over a segmented array where the data vector is all 1, and the flag vector has a true when a new iota begins, which can be determined by an exclusive prefix sum of the shape array. Since our segmented scan is inclusive rather than exclusive, we have to subtract from each element at the end: def segiota [k] (ns: [k]i64) : ?[m].[m]i64 = let m = i64.sum ns let offsets = expresum ns let flags = spread m false offsets (replicate k true) in segscan (+) 0 flags (replicate m 1) |> map (\x -> x - 1) Incidentally, the segmented iota of a shape vector gives the in-segment index for the segmented representation. Essentially, whenever we talk of segmented foo, we mean an operation that intuitively performs the job of maping an operation foo, either consuming or producing a segmented array. As long as these segmented operations follow our rules for what we can turn into efficient (or just executable) GPU code, then we are fine - and you may note that all the segmented operations described so far are fully parallel and completely flat, in the sense that they do not contain any nested parallelism, despite in some sense operating on nested structures. In other fields, a segmented operation is sometimes called a batched operation, although sometimes this implies that the segment sizes are all the same. This is then the core of how Futhark’s new flattening transformation works: use fission to split maps into maps of very simple operations, which temporarily introduces a notion of irregular arrays, then rewrite each of those maps to their corresponding segmented form, which consume and produce arrays in the segmented representation. This means that as long as we have a flattening rule telling us how to generate segmented code for map foo for any possible foo, then we can flatten any program. This is a nice compositional property that means we can treat each language construct in isolation. The next problem, of course, is that some of those foos are mighty tricky. Flattening control flow The trickiest situation occurs when maping a conditional. Futhark’s intermediate representation has some complicated forms of control flow (multiway-branching and loops), but to illustrate the problem and solution, we’ll just deal with a plain if. The problem occurs when we have code like this: map (  x -> if b then foo x else bar x) bs xs Here foo x means some arbitrary code that uses x, not an actual function foo (we’ll get to that problem below). Fission won’t help us further, as the if is not a composition of smaller functions. What we need is a flattening rule for if. The approach we use was invented by Blelloch (as so many things in this field), and is called branch packing. The idea is to partition the iterations of the map into those where the condition is true, and those where the condition is false, execute each of those separately, and combine the results. The price is that we execute both branches separately and spend time partitioning and recombining data. Handwaving a little bit, we flatten code like the above into this: let (xs_true, xs_false) = partition_inputs bs xs let xs_true' = map (\x -> foo x) xs_true let xs_false' = map (\x -> bar x) xs_false let result = combine_inputs bs xs_true' xs_false' In practice, partition_inputs also has to return some auxiliary data that combine_inputs uses to recombine the results in the original order. It’s not hard, just fiddly. The two maps may also need further flattening of course, as foo and bar can be arbitrary code. Loops are handled similar in spirit - keep an array of which iterations of the map have yet to finish, and keep going until they are all done. The shape of the flattened code is an outer loop whose body is parallel. It takes a lot of data movement to repeatedly filter out the ones that are done, so it is not particularly efficient - we’ll look at some more efficient special cases below. Flattening functions But what if foo x really does mean applying the function foo to x? Unsurprisingly, for a functional language, function applications do occur. Although Futhark’s current inlining strategy means we could perhaps ignore them, one of the goals of improving flattening is to eventually be less crude with regards to inlining. The flattening rule for functions is conceptually quite simple: an expression map f xs is flattened to a call to the lifted function f' xs, where f' is generated from f in a systematic manner. The nomenclature of “lifting” is because we “lift” a function of type a -> b to be a function of type []a -> []b, that is, the function f' is “segmented f”. Because we want to deal with segmented arrays, and functions of more than a single argument, the true transformation at the type level is more complicated: each scalar parameter is turned into a (normal) one-dimensional array, and each array parameter is turned into its segmented representation (flag and value vector), and similarly for the return type. The body of the function is then flattened as if it was inside a map nest. It is a very convenient (and to me a little surprising) property that flattening composes so nicely, and it even turns out that recursive functions don’t need any special handling - it just works. This is due to the very nice property that lifting an already lifted function is the lifted function itself, meaning we do not need to generate more than one lifted function, no matter how deeply nested it may occur. At this point in the post, and to the best of my knowledge, we have reproduced Blelloch’s flattening as it existed in NESL in the mid 90s, and which was also implemented for such languages as cuNESL, which compiled a subset of NESL to GPUs years before work began on Futhark. While flattening is (almost) preserving of the time asymptotics of the source program (there are some edge cases for conditionals I won’t get into), the performance on real hardware is not good when flattening is applied naively. The reasons are basically due to locality: flattening tends to increase array sizes asymptotically, and produce a lot of very small parallel kernels, each of which manipulate large arrays in memory. Let us now try to address some of these issues. Cheaper replication Looking under the rug just a bit, we see that one thing I swept under it was how to handle free variables in the functions we map with. I mentioned that as long as we had a flattening rule for map foo for every foo, then we could flatten arbitrary programs, but in the general case foo is a lambda that can access arbitrary variables in scope, like for example this matrix multiplication: let res = map (\xs -> map (\ys -> let zs = map (*) xs ys in reduce (+) 0 zs) yss) xss Applying fission, we are left with this: let zsss = map (\xs -> map (\ys -> map (*) xs ys) yss) xss let res = map (\zss -> map (\zs -> reduce (+) 0 zs) zss) zsss You should note the big three-dimensional zsss array, despite matrix multiplication only involving two-dimensional arrays. This overhead, where the three-dimensional code nesting of the original program results in three-dimensional data nesting in the intermediate results is a common downside of flattening. I usually describe it as flattening turning time into space. It does not affect the asymptotics, as matrix multiplication is already cubic time, but it obviously affects real performance tremendously. In actual Futhark, this issue does not occur, because we do not treat the map and reduce as separate constructs - they are fused into a combined form in the IR, and treated atomically. But as we shall see, that does not solve the entire problem. For simplicity, we do not want our flattening rules to be concerned with free variables. In order to establish the property that a lambda has no free variables, we replicate each free variable and instead pass it as an additional input to each map. Writing rep as a shorthand for replicating the necessary amount, we get: let zsss = map (\xs yss' -> map (\ys xs' -> map (*) xs ys) yss' (rep xs)) xss (rep yss) let res = map (\zss -> map (\zs -> reduce (+) 0 zs) zss) zsss The new parameters have been marked with a prime symbol, and are in some sense only administrative - yss' really is just ys. The reason I don’t just write replicate here is that the arrays to be replicated may in some cases be irregular themselves due to fission, in which case the replication is a segmented replicate - a parallel operation, but a somewhat complicated one. One property of our implementation is that we have not extended the IR in any way. This means that when we generate (say) a segmented iota, we generate a function that contains IR code corresponding to the scans, scatter, etc. that we need. The consequence is that the compiler does not have a high level understanding of the code that is produced by flattening, and it does not understand that fancy segmented replicates can in many cases be simplified away (e.g., indexing a segmented replicate is equivalent to an appropriate indexing of the original array). Perhaps that will change in the future, but for now we have no way to clean up the mess, so perhaps it is better to avoid making a mess in the first place. In our flattening algorithm, we therefore track some arrays as “replicated” using a symbolic representation at compile-time, and handle them specially whenever they are passed as inputs to inner maps. Whenever we would be forced by unfortunate circumstance to actually return these to outside code, we could always manifest them, but this turns out to be needed very rarely. Also, this issue occurs only for variables that are free in a lambda, but bound inside an enclosing map. Variables that are free in the entire nest, such as global variables, need not be replicated. I should note that a different approach to tackling the space blowup issue for flattening is to replace maping of arrays with streaming of sequences, which allows for incrementally producing flattened data, rather than all-at-a-time. This was investigated by Frederik M. Madsen in his PhD thesis. This requires a rather different language (and solving different research problems), so it is not a direction we took. An aside on Data Parallel Haskell Another solution comes from Data Parallel Haskell (DPH) and is discussed in the paper Work efficient higher-order vectorisation, and is based on a different representation of segmented arrays that distinguishes “physical” from “virtual” segments. This differs from Futhark’s implementation in that it also exists at run-time (and is therefore more flexible). As an aside, I will note that DPH is probably the most thorough treatment of flattening since Blelloch’s original work. A lot of the DPH work was highly inspirational to our own efforts, although DPH spent a lot of energy on tackling a richer source language than we are interested in (in particular, they can handle recursive data types). Ultimately, DPH did not perform all that well in practice, and it was ultimately abandoned due to lack of funding. My impression is that DPH struggled because it relied on sophisticated fusion after applying flattening in order to avoid excessive intermediate results, and this fusion optimisation never panned out. Futhark does things slightly differently, in that we aggressively perform fusion before flattening, and then try hard not to fission too much during flattening, such that the flattened code does not need any fancy optimisation (although we still perform low-level memory optimisations, of course). DPH had some very important offshoots however, such as the array libraries Repa and vector, and the embedded language Accelerate. Accelerate in particular is important prior work for Futhark as a whole, as it demonstrated just how nice (and fast) functional array programming can be. Accelerate did not (and does not) support nested parallelism, perhaps because of its authors’ experience with DPH, and this is one reason why support for nested parallelism was such a mark of distinction for Futhark when we first released it. Vectorization avoidance DPH did make one very important observation that we pretty much copied wholesale for Futhark’s flattening. Vectorization avoidance is the idea that sometimes it is more efficient to not flatten something fully. As a slightly contrived demonstration, consider this program: map (\x y -> x * 2 + y * 3 - 1) xs ys This is not what the program actually looks like to Futhark, as the compiler IR uses administrative normal form, a 3AC-like design where arguments to functions (or builtin operations) must be variables or constants. The input to flattening looks more like this: map (\x y -> let a = x * 2 let b = y * 3 let c = a + b let d = c - 1 in d) xs ys We call such let-bindings “statements”. If we aggressively fission this map in order to flatten it, we are left with this: let as = map (\x y -> x * 2) xs ys let bs = map (\y -> y * 3) ys let cs = map (\a b -> a + b) as bs let ds = map (\c -> c - 1) cs If we turn every map into a GPU kernel that reads and writes large arrays in global memory, then we have increased overall memory traffic significantly. Blelloch’s original flattening algorithm did this - partially because it is very principled, and partially because it is amenable to machines where parallel operations can only do a single thing - in practice, NESL compiled to a portable bytecode called VCODE, which had interpreters for various vector machines of the time. (This reminds me that it would be fun to write a VCODE interpreter in Futhark.) However, the issue occurs even without excessive fission. Consider this program: map (  x -> if b then x + 2 else x - 2) bs xs Do we really want to apply the if flattening rule to this, which involves relatively expensive filtering and moving stuff around in memory? No, that would go insufficiently fast. Inspired by DPP, our flattening transformation categorises each statement by whether it is “scalar”, meaning it exhibits no meaningful parallelism, and any arrays it uses are uniform. Uniformity here (and in the next section) means that the size of an array is invariant to the map nest in which it occurs. This is important because it means that fissioning that statement does not result in irregular intermediate arrays, and that if we want to preallocate memory for the statement, we will know its size before executing its map nest. It may be a bit surprising that the rule is not just that something is “scalar” if it involves only primitive (non-array) types, but Futhark programs often contain sequential loops that do sequential things via in-place updates, and it makes no sense to flatten these. We even have some slightly fuzzy heuristics, because it also makes no sense to flatten something like a replicate (even though it is in principle parallel) if it is only used to construct a scratch array that is then operated on completely sequentially. This heuristic may require tweaking in the future - we basically just hammered on it until it behaved reasonably for all of the patterns and benchmarks we could think of. Once statements have been classified, we then group the statements of a lambda by whether they are scalar, and treat sequences of scalar statements as atomic “super-statements” that are not individually fissioned off. This means we can efficiently handle a map that contains both stretches of scalar code, as well as important parallel constructs (like further nested maps) that really need to be fissioned and flattened. All this comes from the nice property that we are free to choose how much to decompose a function into constituent functions, as long as we are willing to live with the consequences of our choice. Exploiting uniformity So far we have mostly looked at how Futhark has replicated known approaches to flattening, with the main tweak being aggressive fusion prior to flattening, and the context of targeting GPU execution, which only cuNESL did previously. But Futhark has one very important advantage that no previous language did: size types, which are present in both the source language and the IR, and which allow program transformations to reason about the symbolic shapes of arrays. In the case of flattening, shape information allows us to distinguish nesting from guaranteed regular to possibly irregular. As a reminder, regular nested parallelism is when the parallel dimensions are uniform in the map nest, meaning invariant to the outer parallel dimensions. When this is the case, we do not need to represent arrays using the segmented representation, but can use normal multi-dimensional arrays. Apart from saving the cost of constructing and the metadata arrays such as the flag vector, this also results in code that is much easier for subsequent compiler passes to analyse. While we have little hope for analysing the result of full flattening (which tends to just be a soup of segmented scans), the Futhark compiler has passes that are able to perform optimisations such as loop tiling on regularly flattened code, but only if it can figure out the looping structure. The uniform case also allows for much simpler flattening rules. The general flattening rule for for-loops is very nasty, in fact so nasty that I could not bring myself to add it to this post, but the flattening rule for a uniform for-loop (where the trip count is also uniform) is quite straightforward. The program fragment map (\xs -> loop xs' = xs for i < k do f xs') xss flattens via loop interchange to loop xss' = xss for i < k do map f xss' but only if f is size-preserving and xss is not irregular. The uniform flattening rule for loops is one of my favourites, because it shows that flattening can to a large extent be seen as a transformation that “pushes the maps” to the innermost level (and vectorization avoidance as a heuristic that makes it not go all the way). Flattening guided by size information is a big win, and we were fortunate that the Futhark compiler already tracked all this information precisely. I remember hearing about other implementations of flattening that got stuck on having to come up with all this size analysis on their own, on an IR that was not designed for it. As of this writing, all Futhark benchmark programs exhibit only regular nested parallelism (because that’s all that used to work!), so handling this efficiently was critical, and I am very pleased that Amirreza (who implemented this part) managed to get it to work as well as I had hoped for. It’s quite the experience to have a speculative plan go this well. All the other stuff from a decade of flattening programs While our old flattener was limited, it was hardly unsophisticated. It was the core of Futhark’s compilation process, and Futhark really is already quite fast in many cases. A new implementation of flattening would have to implement enough of its tricks in order to reach the same performance on real programs. In addition to many heuristics and optimisations, it supported a crucial feature that we call incremental flattening. The idea is that instead of always trying to exploit all parallelism, which may come with overhead, we turn the program into multiple versions, such that each level of each map nest is present in both a sequentialised and flattened version, and at run-time we pick the version that is parallel enough to saturate the hardware, but no more. This is based on the idea that parallelism beyond what the machine can exploit is simply overhead - for example, applying the costly irregular if flattening rule is often not worth the gain of parallelism. Further, sequential code is often subject to locality optimisations, such as loop tiling. Which version is “best” depends on both the program, the workload, and the hardware, and in practice must be determined through an autotuning technique discussed in this paper. Amirreza managed to re-implement incremental flattening using the same technique (and to a degree, the same code) as in our previous work, and it generates all the same versions as before - plus a few more, as we now also treat irregular nesting as parallel (this also causes trouble, more on that below). Incremental flattening not only discriminates based on how much parallelism is exploited, but also on where in the hardware hierarchy it is mapped to. This functionality is core to most instances where Futhark produces truly efficient code, similar to what a human expert would write. It is also part of the new flattening pass, but if you are interested read the pertinent parts of the old blog post as the mechanism is the same. I have hopes for doing optimised flattening inside GPU thread blocks, where the impact of flattening’s less-than-ideal locality is less pronounced, but both the code and the idea will have to wait for a future blog post. The weird performance regressions The goal for the new flattening transformation was to be performance-neutral relative to the old one. In the future we hope to do better, but for now the goal was to do more without anything getting worse. Of course, given that we were replacing a relatively unsystematic transformation with a more principled one, I realised it was impossible for the change to have zero impact, but overall the vast majority of our benchmarks see no change in performance. Initially we did encounter regressions in many programs. The source of this turned out to be irregular nested parallelism that the old flattener would silently treat as sequential, and where treating it as sequential really is the optimal strategy. As an example, consider the following function from the benchmark program hand.fut: def angle_axis_to_rotation_matrix (angle_axis: [3]f64) : [3][3]f64 = let n = f64.sqrt (angle_axis[0] ** 2 + angle_axis[1] ** 2 + angle_axis[2] ** 2) in if n < 0.0001 then identity 3 else let x = angle_axis[0] / n let y = angle_axis[1] / n let z = angle_axis[2] / n let s = f64.sin n let c = f64.cos n in [ [ x * x + (1 - x * x) * c , x * y * (1 - c) - z * s , x * z * (1 - c) + y * s ] , [ x * y * (1 - c) + z * s , y * y + (1 - y * y) * c , y * z * (1 - c) - x * s ] , [ x * z * (1 - c) - y * s , z * y * (1 - c) + x * s , z * z + (1 - z * z) * c ] ] This function is used inside of a map, and since the conditional n < 0.0001 can vary between different iterations of the map, this is a nonuniform if due to control flow, although the size of the array it produces is a uniform [3][3]. The old flattener could not handle nonuniform if in any special way and just turned this entire thing into sequential code, while the new flattener will apply fission and the if flattening rule in order to exploit the parallelism of the identity 3 function call - which constructs a 3x3 identity matrix. The amount of parallelism here is completely irrelevant compared to the bookkeeping cost of flattening if, so this caused a substantial performance regression. Incremental flattening did not save us here, because the function is used in a context where sibling code contains important parallelism, and incremental flattening is all-or-nothing at each level of the map nest. The solution is to add a #[sequential] attribute to the if that indicates to the compiler that it should just be sequentialised. We already use this attribute in other programs to guide incremental flattening along the right paths, or just to cut down on compile time by not generating unnecessary versions. Hence, while using an attribute like this is hardly elegant, it means the new flattener does not need an entirely new workaround when it does the wrong thing - the old workarounds can still be used. Sadly, the attribute solution only works for code the user can see. Futhark also contains a sophisticated implementation of automatic differentiation (real post yet unwritten, but see the documentation and this post). When applying automatic differentiation, the compiler generates substantial and quite complicated code, including various parallel operations, but since it is code that is not written by a human, there is no way for a human to insert attributes. This means we do have one program (hand.fut again, actually) that in its Jacobian computation has up to 2x slowdown on some (not all) workloads, because the adjoint code is overly parallelised. On the other hand, the related benchmark gmm.fut sees a 4x speedup on some Jacobian computations, due to the additional parallelisation of its adjoint code! I played a little bit with our heuristics to see if I could come up with a simple fix, but ultimately decided to leave it until we have a better idea of what the right solution is. This means that there are some programs that will change in performance once the new flattener is merged. How it actually looks I figured some might be curious about what the IR will actually look like post-flattening, so I will provide some examples of flattening here. These are real IR examples, so they are necessarily quite verbose. I have however removed safety checks and source provenance to make it slightly terser. Feel free to skip this section if you dislike reading long reams of tedious machine-generated code (there’ll be enough of that in the future, it seems). Consider this (source) function definition: def f [m] (ns: [m]i64) = map (
 -> i64.sum (iota n)) ns This function contains irregular nested parallelism, as the size n is nonuniform in the map nest. After flattening it will look like this: fun f_7412 (m_7572 : i64, ns_7573 : [m_7572]i64) : {*[m_7572]i64} = { let {m_7777 : i64, segiota_flags_7778 : [m_7777]bool, segiota_offsets_7779 : [m_7572]i64, segiota_elems_7780 : [m_7777]i64} = apply builtin/segiota(m_7572, ns_7573) : {i64, *[?0]bool, *[m_7572]i64, *[?0]i64} let {redomap_7790 : [m_7777]i64} = segscan(thread; ; ) (gtid_7791 < m_7777) (~phys_tid_7792) : {bool, i64} { let {flag_7793 : bool} = segiota_flags_7778[gtid_7791] let {x_7794 : i64} = segiota_elems_7780[gtid_7791] return {returns flag_7793, returns x_7794} } ({false, 0i64}, , \ {x_flag_7795 : bool, eta_p_7796 : i64, y_flag_7797 : bool, eta_p_7798 : i64} : {bool, i64} -> let {x_7799 : bool} = logor(x_flag_7795, y_flag_7797) let {x_7800 : i64} = if y_flag_7797 then {eta_p_7798} else { let {+_res_7801 : i64} = add64(eta_p_7796, eta_p_7798) in {+_res_7801} } : {i64} in {x_7799, x_7800}) \ {seg_flag_7802 : bool, x_7803 : i64} : {i64} -> {x_7803} let {segred_7808 : [m_7572]i64} = segmap(thread; virtualise; ) (gtid_7809 < m_7572) (~phys_tid_7810) : {i64} { let {n_7811 : i64} = ns_7573[gtid_7809] let {cond_7813 : bool} = eq_i64(n_7811, 0i64) let {segment_res_7814 : i64} = if cond_7813 then {0i64} else { let {offset_7812 : i64} = segiota_offsets_7779[gtid_7809] let {binop_x_7816 : i64} = add_nw64(n_7811, offset_7812) let {i_7817 : i64} = sub_nw64(binop_x_7816, 1i64) let {x_7818 : i64} = redomap_7790[i_7817] in {x_7818} } : {i64} return {returns segment_res_7814} } in {segred_7808} } Instead of using map and scan, the IR has dedicated constructs such as segscan and segmap, that can represent multidimensional regular segmented operations. Since this program is irregular, all of these are one-dimensional ((gtid_7809 < m_7572)), and encode the structure using flag arrays. The program first does a segmented iota through a call to a builtin function builtin/segiota, then performs a segmented scan, and finally extracts the last element of each segment. Note that builtin/segiota returns not just the data and flag vectors of the segmented representation, but also an offset vector that denotes the start offset of each segment. This is used in the final segmap. Generally the builtin irregular segmented operations return more than the minimum auxiliary information, because the additional arrays often turn out to be necessary, and usually have to be computed internally anyway. The future The new flattener is not merged yet, but it will be soon. The only work that remains to be done is general simplification and addressing various TODO comments - the performance fluctuations discussed above will be left for the future. In NESL (and DPH), flattening was used to support irregular arrays as a programming construct in the source language. In Futhark, our goals are more modest: we want to support irregular nested parallelism, but we have no plans for adding irregular arrays to the source language or to the IR. Flattening handles irregular intermediate arrays using a bespoke representation that is internal to the flattening pass itself. I am not opposed to irregular arrays in principle, if they can be handled efficiently, but many important Futhark features such as size types and our FFI might get a lot more complicated if we added them. I prefer solving small problems well than big problems poorly, and it has already taken years to solve the problems that arise from Futhark’s fairly small design - and we’re not done yet. I’m not very eager to go looking for even larger problems. That said, I do think we can expose flattening as a programming construct in some way, which will allow for new ways of writing data parallel programs, in particular if we also allow recursion. The main reason for not allowing recursion so far was that we did not have a compilation strategy for recursive functions on GPUs, but the flattening transformation will now move the recursion to the CPU, so this argument does not hold anymore. That, however, is a topic for a future post - this one got long enough.

blocks.html_en: One of the most interesting implementation challenges in Futhark is how to map nested parallelism, in which parallel operations can contain other parallel operations, to flat parallelism. This challenge arises because much interesting hardware (such as GPUs) does not efficiently support nested parallelism, and even on CPUs, arbitrary nesting may have significant run-time costs. Futhark has for a long time supported flattening only a limited (although important) subset of programs, called regular nested parallelism (as opposed to irregular), which meant that there were programs that we were unable to compile to GPU code. In 2022 I began an experimental implementation of “full flattening”, which as of this writing is the longest open pull request on the Futhark repository. I got far enough to build a proof of concept, but the sheer amount of effort involved led to the work stagnating - until now. Largely due to the efforts of students, we are now close to having a complete reimplementation of flattening in Futhark.

blocks.html_en: (The rule is more convoluted once multiple input arrays are allowed, but let us ignore that.) Usually we apply the rule left-to-right in order to perform fusion and avoid having to store intermediate arrays in memory, but we can also apply it right-to-left, in which case it provides us a way to decompose complex maps into sequences of trivial maps that just perform one single operation (or a compound one - we can apply fission to the degree we want, which I will return to). This is the main technique we use for cutting apart an arbitrarily complex data parallel program into smaller manageable chunks. blocks.html_en: This issue is the root of the limitation on our original flattening transformation, which is that it cannot handle irregular nested parallelism, meaning parallelism of a size that varies between iterations of outer parallel dimensions. In the example above, m is local to the outermost map, so the iota and reduce (both of which have a parallel width of m) are irregular. Our only choice would then be to sequentialise this code. Now, in the actual compiler, the iota would be fused into the reduce (using a representation I will not go into), but if we ignore that part, it seems like we are violating one of our constraints, which is that all memory for intermediate results must be preallocated - and here we need an array of size m, where m can be different for each thread. In this case, the problem can be solved by an inspector that extracts a slice of the program that computes all intermediate sizes (but not any other values), which is then used to compute memory requirements and organise intermediate results in memory. blocks.html_en: The flattening rule for functions is conceptually quite simple: an expression map f xs is flattened to a call to the lifted function f' xs, where f' is generated from f in a systematic manner. The nomenclature of “lifting” is because we “lift” a function of type a -> b to be a function of type []a -> []b, that is, the function f' is “segmented f”. Because we want to deal with segmented arrays, and functions of more than a single argument, the true transformation at the type level is more complicated: each scalar parameter is turned into a (normal) one-dimensional array, and each array parameter is turned into its segmented representation (flag and value vector), and similarly for the return type. The body of the function is then flattened as if it was inside a map nest.

blocks.html_en: In the case of flattening, shape information allows us to distinguish nesting from guaranteed regular to possibly irregular. As a reminder, regular nested parallelism is when the parallel dimensions are uniform in the map nest, meaning invariant to the outer parallel dimensions. When this is the case, we do not need to represent arrays using the segmented representation, but can use normal multi-dimensional arrays. Apart from saving the cost of constructing and the metadata arrays such as the flag vector, this also results in code that is much easier for subsequent compiler passes to analyse. While we have little hope for analysing the result of full flattening (which tends to just be a soup of segmented scans), the Futhark compiler has passes that are able to perform optimisations such as loop tiling on regularly flattened code, but only if it can figure out the looping structure.

blocks.html_en: While our old flattener was limited, it was hardly unsophisticated. It was the core of Futhark’s compilation process, and Futhark really is already quite fast in many cases. A new implementation of flattening would have to implement enough of its tricks in order to reach the same performance on real programs.

blocks.html_en: In addition to many heuristics and optimisations, it supported a crucial feature that we call incremental flattening. The idea is that instead of always trying to exploit all parallelism, which may come with overhead, we turn the program into multiple versions, such that each level of each map nest is present in both a sequentialised and flattened version, and at run-time we pick the version that is parallel enough to saturate the hardware, but no more. This is based on the idea that parallelism beyond what the machine can exploit is simply overhead - for example, applying the costly irregular if flattening rule is often not worth the gain of parallelism. Further, sequential code is often subject to locality optimisations, such as loop tiling. Which version is “best” depends on both the program, the workload, and the hardware, and in practice must be determined through an autotuning technique discussed in this paper.

blocks.html_en: This function is used inside of a map, and since the conditional n < 0.0001 can vary between different iterations of the map, this is a nonuniform if due to control flow, although the size of the array it produces is a uniform [3][3]. The old flattener could not handle nonuniform if in any special way and just turned this entire thing into sequential code, while the new flattener will apply fission and the if flattening rule in order to exploit the parallelism of the identity 3 function call - which constructs a 3x3 identity matrix. The amount of parallelism here is completely irrelevant compared to the bookkeeping cost of flattening if, so this caused a substantial performance regression. blocks.html_en: Sadly, the attribute solution only works for code the user can see. Futhark also contains a sophisticated implementation of automatic differentiation (real post yet unwritten, but see the documentation and this post). When applying automatic differentiation, the compiler generates substantial and quite complicated code, including various parallel operations, but since it is code that is not written by a human, there is no way for a human to insert attributes. This means we do have one program (hand.fut again, actually) that in its Jacobian computation has up to 2x slowdown on some (not all) workloads, because the adjoint code is overly parallelised. On the other hand, the related benchmark gmm.fut sees a 4x speedup on some Jacobian computations, due to the additional parallelisation of its adjoint code! I played a little bit with our heuristics to see if I could come up with a simple fix, but ultimately decided to leave it until we have a better idea of what the right solution is. This means that there are some programs that will change in performance once the new flattener is merged.

blocks.html_en: Instead of using map and scan, the IR has dedicated constructs such as segscan and segmap, that can represent multidimensional regular segmented operations. Since this program is irregular, all of these are one-dimensional ((gtid_7809 < m_7572)), and encode the structure using flag arrays. blocks.html_en: In NESL (and DPH), flattening was used to support irregular arrays as a programming construct in the source language. In Futhark, our goals are more modest: we want to support irregular nested parallelism, but we have no plans for adding irregular arrays to the source language or to the IR. Flattening handles irregular intermediate arrays using a bespoke representation that is internal to the flattening pass itself. I am not opposed to irregular arrays in principle, if they can be handled efficiently, but many important Futhark features such as size types and our FFI might get a lot more complicated if we added them. I prefer solving small problems well than big problems poorly, and it has already taken years to solve the problems that arise from Futhark’s fairly small design - and we’re not done yet. I’m not very eager to go looking for even larger problems.

content_html_zh:
发表于 2026 年 7 月 31 日

底线：这篇长博文描述了我们长达数年努力的成果，这意味着我们现在可以在模编译器错误和一些不重要的边缘情况下，将任何 Futhark 程序编译为并行 GPU 代码。

介绍

Futhark 最有趣的实现挑战之一是如何将嵌套并行（其中并行操作可以包含其他并行操作）映射到平面并行。 出现这一挑战的原因是许多有趣的硬件（例如 GPU）无法有效地支持嵌套并行性，甚至在 CPU 上，任意嵌套也可能会产生巨大的运行时成本。 Futhark 长期以来只支持扁平化有限（尽管很重要）的程序子集，称为常规嵌套并行性（而不是不规则并行性），这意味着有些程序我们无法编译为 GPU 代码。 2022 年，我开始实验性地实现“完全扁平化”，截至撰写本文时，这是 Futhark 存储库上最长的开放拉取请求。 我已经取得了足够的进展来构建概念验证，但所涉及的大量工作导致工作停滞不前 - 直到现在。 很大程度上由于学生们的努力，我们现在即将在 Futhark 中完全重新实现扁平化。

主要贡献来自 Cornelius Sevald-Krause，他在他的理学士学位论文中实现了函数和匹配提升，特别是 Amirreza Hashemi，他的理科硕士工作就像旋风一样完成了其他所有事情。 这包括各种关键的优化，以达到与旧的拼合器相同的功能和性能。 我无法夸大为一个十年前的充满优化启发式的编译器过程提供一个系统且可维护的替代方案是多么令人印象深刻。

这篇文章将介绍扁平化的基本问题，讨论一些各种挑战，并解释我们如何在即将合并的 Futhark 编译器工作中解决这些问题。 扁平化有着悠久的学术渊源，我会尝试将相关的其他工作联系起来，但这篇文章并不是对先前工作的系统调查。 我将忽略编译器实际实现所有这些内容所需执行的大部分重要簿记工作，而是专注于程序如何转换的直觉。

我应该提前提到这项工作的目标是什么：新的扁平化转换不应该降低已经与旧实现一起工作的程序的性能，但我们不太关心以前不起作用的程序的性能。 正如我们将看到的，在任意不规则的嵌套并行性上实现真正良好的性能本身就是一个主要的研究问题，也是我们打算在未来逐步解决的一个问题。

另外，这是一篇很长的文章。 我试图让这里的所有内容都相对较高水平，但如果事情拖得太长，不符合您的口味，您可能想跳到底部的思考。

展平的基础知识

为了促进扁平化，我们将对 GPU 的功能进行略微讽刺的假设。 扩展到完整的 GPU 功能并不会从根本上改变情况；这只是意味着我需要更复杂的例子。 此外，尽管这篇文章重点关注 GPU，但您可以在心里用“高效但受限的处理器”来代替 - 这些问题会在任何类型的矢量处理中出现。

在函数式编程语言中，我们首先假设 GPU 可以有效地执行映射，其中函数包含顺序代码，并且可以提前分配用于中间结果的所有内存。 为了避免一直编写 zip/unzip，我们还假设我们的映射接受任意数量的数组。 例如，我们可以在 GPU 上高效地执行以下操作：

map (\x y -> x + y) xs ys

（顺便说一句，在描述要遵循的转换时，如果 map 在 lambda 之前接受其数组，就会简单得多，就像我们在 Futhark 的 IR 中所做的那样 - 但我不想在博客文章中走得那么远。）

很容易想象，这可以变成一个 GPU 程序，每次地图迭代都有一个线程。 除了具有顺序代码的单个映射之外，我们还允许任何映射嵌套。 所以这也是有效的：

map (\xs ys -> map (\x y -> x + y)
                   xs ys)
    xss yss

同样很容易想象这些地图可以折叠，最里面地图的每次迭代都有一个 GPU 线程。

除了任意顺序代码之外，我们还允许最里面的操作是单个并行操作，例如扫描、归约、转置——精确的集合并不重要。 那么这也是有效的：

map (\xs -> reduce (+) 0 xs)
    xs

本质上，“高效 GPU 代码”意味着在某些单个并行基元操作（或顺序代码）之上的映射塔。 这些模式之所以高效，是因为我们知道如何从这些模式生成高效的 GPU 内核。 这与骨架有一定关系，但我们通常不使用该术语，因为我们打算使用这些模式作为编译器的推理机制，而不是用户可见的编程模型。 在实际的编译器中，我们当然有专用的构造来可靠地表达“其中包含特定内容的映射”，但为了最大限度地减少本文中的语法，我将主要坚持使用映射塔。

当然，Futhark 程序员可能不会编写看起来像那样的程序。 这样大胆、思想自由的人可能会这样写：

map (\xs -> let y = reduce (+) 0 xs
            let zs = map (+y) xs
            in zs)
    xss

这确实符合我们讨论的模式之一：如果我们放弃内部映射的并行性并进行归约，那么这是一个包含顺序代码的映射。 在编译并行语言时，这是一个重要的选择：您不必利用所有并行性。 从语义上讲，大多数并行语言并不需要并行执行才能正确；这只是实施可以采取的一种选择。 当然，我们不应该太过分——不利用任何并行性的并行语言很可能会被指控违反契约。

在这种情况下，我们可以将程序重写为语义相同但以有效模式表示的程序。 为了弄清楚发生了什么，首先让我们添加一些类型注释，其中我们假设 xs 的形状为 [n][m]：

map (\xs -> let y : i32 = reduce (+) 0 xs
            let zs : [m]i32 = map (+y) xs
            in zs)
    xss

然后我们将外部映射分成两个单独的映射，第一个映射返回传递到第二个映射的中间结果数组：

let ys =
  map (\xs -> reduce (+) 0 xs)
      xss
let zss =
  map (\xs y -> map (+y) xs)
      xss ys

现在，这两个映射与我们知道如何转化为高效 GPU 代码的模式相匹配。 我们在这里所做的转换通常称为循环分布或裂变，并且是循环融合的对应部分。 对于纯函数式语言，以下等式成立：

map f ∘ map g = map (f∘g)

（一旦允许多个输入数组，规则就会更加复杂，但让我们忽略它。） 通常我们从左到右应用规则，以便执行融合并避免在内存中存储中间数组，但我们也可以从右到左应用它，在这种情况下，它为我们提供了一种将复杂映射分解为仅执行单个操作的简单映射序列的方法（或复合操作 - 我们可以将裂变应用到我们想要的程度，我将返回）。 这是我们用来将任意复杂的数据并行程序分割成更小的可管理块的主要技术。 据我所知，它是 Guy Blelloch 在 90 年代初作为他在 NESL 工作的一部分而首创的，尽管它有时被称为“矢量化”，因为它的输出在完全应用时由地图和扫描组成，内部有一些琐碎的操作，可以被视为“矢量操作”。 然而，在我们拥有有效的扁平化算法的所有组件之前，我们仍然需要解决两个主要问题。

不规则中间阵列

考虑这个程序：

map (\m -> let xs : [m]i64 = iota m
           let y : i64 = reduce (+) 0 xs
           in y)
    ns

回想一下 iota m 生成一个大小为 m 的数组 [0, ..., m-1]。 该程序具有与上述相同的问题，即并行操作没有完美嵌套。 那么让我们尝试裂变（fise？） 地图：

let xss : [n][???]i64 =
  map (\n -> iota n)
      ns
let ys =
  map (\xs -> reduce (+) 0 xs)
      xss

请注意 xss 绑定类型中的问号 - 我们应该在那里放置什么大小？ 直观上，操作映射 (\n -> iota n) ns 生成一个不规则数组，其中行具有不同的大小，具体取决于输入数组 ns 的值。 人们可能期望 map (\n -> iota n) [1,2,3] 生成数组 [[0],[0,1],[0,1,2]]，但不幸的是，Futhark 不允许不规则数组；既不在源语言中，也不在我们的 IR 中。 原因是性能驱动的，因为一旦你有不规则的数组，你要么需要将数组表示为指针数组，要么丢失随机访问索引。 当您想要以矢量处理器为目标时，这两种方法都不令人满意。 这意味着我们不想在源语言和 IR 中允许不规则数组。

这个问题是我们原始展平变换的局限性的根源，即它无法处理不规则的嵌套并行性，即大小在外部并行维度的迭代之间变化的并行性。 在上面的例子中，m是最外层map的局部，因此iota和reduce（两者的平行宽度均为m）是不规则的。 我们唯一的选择就是对这段代码进行排序。 现在，在实际的编译器中，iota 将被融合到reduce 中（使用我不会讨论的表示），但如果我们忽略该部分，似乎我们违反了我们的约束之一，即中间结果的所有内存必须预先分配 - 这里我们需要一个大小为 m 的数组，其中每个线程的 m 可以不同。 在这种情况下，问题可以通过检查器来解决，该检查器提取计算所有中间大小（但不是任何其他值）的程序片段，然后将其用于计算内存需求并在内存中组织中间结果。 有时可以这样做（大致上，当顺序循环没有棘手的业务时），但这是一种尽力而为的事情，并且它不会恢复并行性。

无论如何，处理不规则数组的能力显然对于处理不规则嵌套并行性的总体目标至关重要。 解决方案是将不规则数组表示为平面（一维数组），这仍然允许并行执行我们需要的操作。 中心构建块是将二维不规则数组编码为数据向量和标志向量，两者大小相同。 数据向量只是数组的行连接，而标志向量指示其对应元素是否是新行的开头。 例子：

  • 嵌套不规则数组：[[1], [2,3], [4,5,6]]
  • 值向量：[1,2,3,4,5,6]
  • 标志向量：[真，真，假，真，假，假]

（对二维数组的限制不失一般性：我们总是可以折叠额外的内部维度并让辅助数组告诉我们如何重建它们。 为了简单起见，我们不会进一步详细介绍。）

我们称其为分段数组，“不规则行”称为段。 上面的数组有三个段，大小分别为 1、2 和 3。 在实践中，我们经常使用某些额外的辅助数组，用于跟踪每个段的大小（形状向量，在本例中为[1,2,3]）、每个段在数据向量中的起始偏移量（此处为偏移向量，[0,1,3]），以及将数据数组的每个元素与其段索引（[0,1,1,2,2,2]）和段内索引（[0,0,1,0,1,2]）相关联的数组。 然而，这些都可以从标志向量有效地计算出来。

这种表示的基本操作是分段扫描，它可以根据标准扫描定义如下：

def segscan 't [n]
            (op: t -> t -> t)
            (ne: t)
            (flags: [n]bool)
            (vals: [n]t) : [n]t =
  let pairs =
    scan (\(v1, f1) (v2, f2) ->
            let f = f1 || f2
            let v = if f2 then v2 else op v1 v2
            in (v, f))
         (ne, false)
         (zip vals flags)
  let (res, _) = unzip pairs
  in res

我们可以将其应用于上面的不规则数组的表示，以获得（包含）扫描每个段的结果，并将其连接成单个数组：

> segscan (+) 0 [true, true, false, true, false, false]
                       [1,2,3,4,5,6]
[1, 2, 5, 4, 9, 15]

这是表示 [1,2,5]++[4,9]++[15] 的分段数组的值数组，使用未更改的原始标志数组。 由于扫描是并行算法中如此重要的构建块，因此一旦我们可以扫描这些分段数组，我们就可以做各种其他事情也就不足为奇了。 例如，我们可以通过首先执行分段扫描，然后提取每个扫描段的最终元素来进行分段归约：

def segreduce 't [n]
              (op: t -> t -> t)
              (ne: t)
              (flags: [n]bool)
              (vals: [n]t) : ?[m].[m]t =
  segscan op ne flags vals
  |> zip (rotate 1 flags)
  |> filter (.0)
  |> map (.1)
> segreduce (+) 0 [true, true, false, true, false, false]
                         [1,2,3,4,5,6]
[1, 5, 15]

类似地，我们可以构造一个分段的 iota，它将 []i64 类型的形状向量作为输入，并在道德上将 iota 映射到该数组上。 该构造基于以下观察：正常的 iota 可以写为包含 n 个 1 副本的数组上的独占前缀和：

def iota n = expresum (replicate n 1)

那么分段的iota只是对分段数组的分段扫描，其中数据向量全为1，并且当新的iota开始时标志向量为真，这可以通过形状数组的独占前缀和来确定。 由于我们的分段扫描是包容性的而不是排他性的，所以我们必须从最后的每个元素中减去：

def segiota [k] (ns: [k]i64) : ?[m].[m]i64 =
  let m = i64.sum ns
  let offsets = expresum ns
  let flags = spread m false offsets (replicate k true)
  in segscan (+) 0 flags (replicate m 1)
     |> map (\x -> x - 1)

顺便说一句，形状向量的分段 iota 给出了分段表示的分段内索引。

本质上，每当我们谈论分段 foo 时，我们指的是直观地执行映射操作 foo 的工作的操作，即消耗或生成分段数组。 只要这些分段操作遵循我们可以转化为高效（或可执行）GPU 代码的规则，那么我们就可以了 - 您可能会注意到，到目前为止描述的所有分段操作都是完全并行和完全平坦的，从某种意义上说，它们不包含任何嵌套并行性，尽管在某种意义上是在嵌套结构上操作。 在其他领域，分段操作有时称为批处理操作，尽管有时这意味着段大小都是相同的。

这就是 Futhark 新的扁平化变换工作原理的核心：使用裂变将映射拆分为非常简单操作的映射，这暂时引入了不规则数组的概念，然后将每个映射重写为其相应的分段形式，从而以分段表示形式消耗和生成数组。 这意味着只要我们有一个扁平化规则告诉我们如何为任何可能的 foo 生成映射 foo 的分段代码，那么我们就可以扁平化任何程序。 这是一个很好的组合属性，意味着我们可以单独对待每种语言构造。

当然，下一个问题是其中一些 foo 非常棘手。

扁平化控制流程

最棘手的情况发生在映射条件时。 Futhark 的中间表示有一些复杂形式的控制流（多路分支和循环），但为了说明问题和解决方案，我们只处理一个简单的 if。 当我们有这样的代码时就会出现问题：

map (\b x -> if b then foo x
                  else bar x)
    bs xs

这里 foo x 表示一些使用 x 的任意代码，而不是实际的函数 foo （我们将在下面讨论这个问题）。 Fission 不会为我们提供更多帮助，因为 if 不是较小函数的组合。 我们需要的是 if 的扁平化规则。

我们使用的方法是由 Blelloch 发明的（正如该领域的许多事情一样），称为分支打包。 这个想法是将映射的迭代划分为条件为真的迭代和条件为假的迭代，分别执行每个迭代，然后组合结果。 代价是我们分别执行两个分支并花费时间分区和重新组合数据。 稍微挥手一下，我们将上面的代码扁平化为：

let (xs_true, xs_false) = partition_inputs bs xs
let xs_true' = map (\x -> foo x) xs_true
let xs_false' = map (\x -> bar x) xs_false
let result = combine_inputs bs xs_true' xs_false'

实际上，partition_inputs 还必须返回一些辅助数据，combine_inputs 使用这些数据按原始顺序重新组合结果。 这并不难，只是繁琐。 当然，这两个映射可能还需要进一步扁平化，因为 foo 和 bar 可以是任意代码。

循环的处理在本质上是类似的 - 保留一个数组，其中映射的迭代尚未完成，并继续下去，直到它们全部完成。 扁平码的形状是一个外环，其主体是平行的。 需要大量的数据移动来重复过滤掉已完成的数据，因此效率不是特别高 - 我们将在下面看看一些更高效的特殊情况。

展平函数

但如果 foo x 确实意味着将函数 foo 应用于 x 呢？ 毫不奇怪，对于函数式语言来说，函数应用确实会发生。 尽管 Futhark 当前的内联策略意味着我们可能会忽略它们，但改进扁平化的目标之一是最终在内联方面变得不那么粗糙。

函数的扁平化规则在概念上非常简单：表达式映射 f xs 被扁平化为对提升函数 f' xs 的调用，其中 f' 是以系统方式从 f 生成的。 “提升”的命名是因为我们将 a -> b 类型的函数“提升”为 []a -> []b 类型的函数，即函数 f' 是“分段的 f”。 因为我们想要处理分段数组和多个参数的函数，所以类型级别的真正转换更加复杂：每个标量参数都转换为（正常）一维数组，每个数组参数转换为其分段表示形式（标志和值向量），对于返回类型也是如此。 然后函数体被展平，就像它位于地图嵌套内一样。

这是一个非常方便（对我来说有点令人惊讶）的属性，扁平化组合得如此之好，甚至事实证明递归函数不需要任何特殊处理 - 它就可以工作。 这是由于一个非常好的属性，即提升已经提升的函数就是提升的函数本身，这意味着我们不需要生成多个提升的函数，无论它的嵌套有多深。

就我所知，在这篇文章的这一点上，我们已经重现了 Blelloch 的扁平化，因为它存在于 90 年代中期的 NESL 中，并且它也被用于 cuNESL 等语言，它在 Futhark 的工作开始之前几年将 NESL 的子集编译到 GPU。 虽然扁平化（几乎）保留了源程序的时间渐进性（条件条件有一些边缘情况我不会讨论），但当简单地应用扁平化时，实际硬件上的性能并不好。 原因基本上是由于局部性：展平往往会渐近地增加数组大小，并产生许多非常小的并行内核，每个内核都操作内存中的大型数组。 现在让我们尝试解决其中一些问题。

更便宜的复制

稍微深入了解一下，我们发现我所关心的一件事是如何处理我们映射的函数中的自由变量。 我提到过，只要我们对每个 foo 的映射 foo 有一个扁平化规则，那么我们就可以扁平化任意程序，但在一般情况下 foo 是一个可以访问范围内任意变量的 lambda，例如这个矩阵乘法：

let res =
  map (\xs -> map (\ys -> let zs = map (*) xs ys
                          in reduce (+) 0 zs)
                  yss)
      xss

应用裂变，我们剩下这个：

let zsss = map (\xs -> map (\ys -> map (*) xs ys) yss) xss
let res =
  map (\zss -> map (\zs -> reduce (+) 0 zs)
                   zss)
      zsss

您应该注意大的三维 zsss 数组，尽管矩阵乘法仅涉及二维数组。 这种开销（原始程序的三维代码嵌套导致中间结果中的三维数据嵌套）是扁平化的常见缺点。 我通常将其描述为将时间扁平化为空间。 它不会影响渐近，因为矩阵乘法已经是三次时间，但它显然极大地影响了实际性能。

在实际的 Futhark 中，这个问题不会发生，因为我们不将映射和归约视为单独的构造 - 它们在 IR 中融合成组合形式，并以原子方式处理。 但正如我们将看到的，这并不能解决全部问题。

为简单起见，我们不希望我们的展平规则与自由变量有关。 为了建立 lambda 没有自由变量的属性，我们复制每个自由变量，并将其作为附加输入传递给每个映射。 将rep写为复制必要数量的简写，我们得到：

let zsss = map (\xs yss' -> map (\ys xs' -> map (*) xs ys) yss' (rep xs))
               xss (rep yss)
let res =
  map (\zss -> map (\zs -> reduce (+) 0 zs)
                   zss)
      zsss

新参数已标有撇号，并且在某种意义上只是管理性的 - yss' 实际上只是 ys。 我在这里不只写复制的原因是，在某些情况下，要复制的数组可能由于裂变而本身不规则，在这种情况下，复制是分段复制——一种并行操作，但有点复杂。

我们实施的一个特点是我们没有以任何方式扩展 IR。 这意味着，当我们生成（例如）分段 iota 时，我们会生成一个函数，其中包含与我们需要的扫描、分散等相对应的 IR 代码。 结果是编译器对扁平化生成的代码没有高层次的理解，并且它不明白在许多情况下可以简化花哨的分段复制（例如，对分段复制进行索引相当于对原始数组进行适当的索引）。 也许这种情况将来会改变，但现在我们没有办法收拾残局，所以也许一开始就避免弄乱会更好。

因此，在我们的展平算法中，我们在编译时使用符号表示来跟踪一些“复制”的数组，并在它们作为输入传递到内部映射时专门处理它们。 每当我们因不幸的情况而被迫将它们实际返回给外部代码时，我们总是可以将它们显现出来，但事实证明很少需要这样做。 此外，此问题仅发生在 lambda 中自由但绑定在封闭映射内的变量上。 整个嵌套中空闲的变量，例如全局变量，不需要复制。

我应该注意到，解决扁平化空间爆炸问题的另一种方法是用序列流代替数组映射，这允许增量生成扁平化数据，而不是一次性生成。 Frederik M.对此进行了调查。 马德森在他的博士论文中。 这需要一种相当不同的语言（并解决不同的研究问题），所以这不是我们采取的方向。

关于数据并行 Haskell 的旁白

另一个解决方案来自 Data Parallel Haskell (DPH)，并在论文《工作高效高阶向量化》中进行了讨论，该解决方案基于区分“物理”段和“虚拟”段的分段数组的不同表示。 这与 Futhark 的实现不同，因为它也存在于运行时（因此更灵活）。 顺便说一句，我要指出的是，DPH 可能是自 Blelloch 的原创作品以来最彻底的扁平化处理方法。 尽管 DPH 花费了大量精力来处理比我们感兴趣的更丰富的源语言（特别是它们可以处理递归数据类型），但 DPH 的许多工作对我们自己的努力非常有启发。

最终，DPH 在实践中表现不佳，最终因缺乏资金而被放弃。 我的印象是，DPH 陷入了困境，因为它在应用扁平化后依赖于复杂的融合，以避免过多的中间结果，而这种融合优化从未成功。 Futhark 的做法略有不同，因为我们在扁平化之前积极执行融合，然后在扁平化期间努力不要分裂太多，这样扁平化的代码就不需要任何花哨的优化（当然，尽管我们仍然执行低级内存优化）。

然而，DPH 有一些非常重要的分支，例如数组库 Repa 和 Vector，以及嵌入式语言 Accelerate。 对于 Futhark 整体来说，加速尤其重要，因为它展示了函数式数组编程是多么的好（和快）。 Accelerate 不支持嵌套并行性，也许是因为其作者在 DPH 方面的经验，这也是为什么当我们第一次发布 Futhark 时，支持嵌套并行性是 Futhark 的一个显着特征。

避免矢量化

DPH 确实做出了一项非常重要的观察，我们几乎批量复制了 Futhark 的扁平化。 避免矢量化是指有时不完全展平某些东西会更有效。 作为一个稍微做作的演示，请考虑以下程序：

map (\x y -> x * 2 + y * 3 - 1)
    xs ys

对于 Futhark 来说，这并不是程序的实际样子，因为编译器 IR 使用管理范式，这是一种类似 3AC 的设计，其中函数（或内置操作）的参数必须是变量或常量。 扁平化的输入看起来更像是这样的：

map (\x y -> let a = x * 2
             let b = y * 3
             let c = a + b
             let d = c - 1
             in d)
    xs ys

我们将这种 let 绑定称为“语句”。 如果我们积极地裂变这张地图以使其变平，我们就会得到这样的结果：

let as = map (\x y -> x * 2) xs ys
let bs = map (\y -> y * 3) ys
let cs = map (\a b -> a + b) as bs
let ds = map (\c -> c - 1) cs

如果我们将每个映射变成一个 GPU 内核，在全局内存中读取和写入大型数组，那么我们就显着增加了总体内存流量。 Blelloch 最初的扁平化算法做到了这一点——部分是因为它非常有原则性，部分是因为它适用于并行操作只能做单一事情的机器——在实践中，NESL 编译成一种名为 VCODE 的可移植字节码，它具有适用于当时各种向量机的解释器。 （这让我想起用 Futhark 编写一个 VCODE 解释器会很有趣。）

然而，即使没有过度裂变，也会出现该问题。 考虑这个程序：

map (\b x -> if b then x + 2 else x - 2) bs xs

我们真的想应用 if 扁平化规则吗？这涉及到相对昂贵的过滤和在内存中移动内容？ 不，那样会进展不够快。

受 DPP 的启发，我们的展平变换根据每个语句是否是“标量”对它进行分类，这意味着它没有表现出有意义的并行性，并且它使用的任何数组都是统一的。 这里（以及下一节）的一致性意味着数组的大小对于它所在的映射嵌套是不变的。 这很重要，因为这意味着分裂该语句不会导致不规则的中间数组，并且如果我们想为该语句预分配内存，我们将在执行其映射嵌套之前知道其大小。

可能有点令人惊讶的是，该规则不仅仅是如果某事物仅涉及原始（非数组）类型，那么它就是“标量”，而且 Futhark 程序通常包含通过就地更新执行顺序操作的顺序循环，并且展平这些是没有意义的。 我们甚至有一些稍微模糊的启发法，因为如果它仅用于构造一个临时数组，然后完全按顺序操作，那么将诸如复制之类的东西展平（即使它原则上是并行的）也是没有意义的。 这种启发式方法可能需要在未来进行调整——我们基本上只是不断地锤炼它，直到它对于我们能想到的所有模式和基准都表现得合理为止。

一旦语句被分类，我们就会根据 lambda 语句是否是标量对它们进行分组，并将标量语句序列视为不会单独分裂的原子“超级语句”。 这意味着我们可以有效地处理包含标量代码片段以及真正需要裂变和展平的重要并行结构（如进一步嵌套的映射）的映射。 所有这一切都来自于一个很好的特性，即我们可以自由选择将函数分解为组成函数的程度，只要我们愿意承担我们选择的后果。

利用均匀性

到目前为止，我们主要研究了 Futhark 如何复制已知的扁平化方法，主要调整是扁平化之前的积极融合，以及针对 GPU 执行的上下文，这之前只有 cuNESL 做过。 但 Futhark 有一个以前的语言没有的非常重要的优势：大小类型，它存在于源语言和 IR 中，并且允许程序转换来推理数组的符号形状。

在展平的情况下，形状信息使我们能够区分嵌套是保证规则的还是可能不规则的。 提醒一下，常规嵌套并行是指映射嵌套中的平行尺寸是统一的，这意味着对于外部平行尺寸而言是不变的。 在这种情况下，我们不需要使用分段表示来表示数组，而是可以使用普通的多维数组。 除了节省构建成本和元数据数组（例如标志向量）之外，这还可以使后续编译器更容易分析代码。 虽然我们对分析完全扁平化的结果（这往往只是分段扫描的汤）的希望不大，但 Futhark 编译器具有能够执行优化的通道，例如对常规扁平化代码进行循环平铺，但前提是它能够找出循环结构。

统一的情况还允许更简单的扁平化规则。 for 循环的一般扁平化规则非常令人讨厌，事实上，太讨厌了，以至于我无法将其添加到这篇文章中，但是统一 for 循环的扁平化规则（其中行程计数也是统一的）非常简单。 程序片段

map (\xs -> loop xs' = xs for i < k do
              f xs')
    xss

通过循环交换变平为

loop xss' = xss for i < k do
  map f xss'

但前提是 f 保持尺寸不变并且 xss 不规则。

循环的统一扁平化规则是我最喜欢的规则之一，因为它表明扁平化在很大程度上可以被视为一种将“映射”推到最内层的转换（而避免矢量化作为一种​​启发式方法，使其无法一路顺利）。

由大小信息引导的扁平化是一个巨大的胜利，我们很幸运，Futhark 编译器已经精确地跟踪了所有这些信息。 我记得听说过其他扁平化的实现，它们必须自己在不是为此设计的 IR 上进行所有这些尺寸分析。 截至撰写本文时，所有 Futhark 基准程序都仅表现出常规的嵌套并行性（因为这就是过去所有的工作方式！），因此有效地处理这一问题至关重要，而且我很高兴 Amirreza（实现了这部分）设法使其按照我的预期工作。 一个投机计划进展得这么顺利，真是一种体验。

十年扁平化计划中的所有其他内容

虽然我们的旧压平机功能有限，但它并不简单。 它是 Futhark 编译过程的核心，而且 Futhark 在很多情况下确实已经相当快了。 扁平化的新实现必须实现足够的技巧才能在实际程序上达到相同的性能。

除了许多启发式方法和优化之外，它还支持一个关键功能，我们称之为增量扁平化。 我们的想法是，我们不是总是尝试利用所有并行性（这可能会带来开销），而是将程序转换为多个版本，以便每个映射嵌套的每个级别都以顺序化和扁平化版本的形式出现，并且在运行时我们选择并行性足以使硬件饱和的版本，但仅此而已。 这是基于这样的想法：超出机器可以利用的并行性只是开销 - 例如，应用昂贵的不规则 if 扁平化规则通常不值得并行性的增益。 此外，顺序代码通常需要进行局部优化，例如循环平铺。 哪个版本“最好”取决于程序、工作负载和硬件，并且在实践中必须通过本文讨论的自动调整技术来确定。

Amirreza 设法使用与我们之前的工作相同的技术（在某种程度上，相同的代码）重新实现增量扁平化，并且它生成与以前相同的所有版本 - 加上更多版本，因为我们现在也将不规则嵌套视为并行（这也会引起麻烦，下面将详细介绍）。

增量扁平化不仅基于并行性的利用程度，还基于并行性映射到硬件层次结构中的位置。 此功能是 Futhark 生成真正高效代码的大多数实例的核心，类似于人类专家编写的代码。 它也是新的扁平化过程的一部分，但如果您有兴趣，请阅读旧博客文章的相关部分，因为机制是相同的。

我希望在 GPU 线程块内进行优化扁平化，其中扁平化不太理想的局部性的影响不太明显，但代码和想法都必须等待未来的博客文章。

奇怪的性能回归

新的扁平化转型的目标是相对于旧的扁平化转型保持性能中立。 未来我们希望做得更好，但目前的目标是在不让事情变得更糟的情况下做得更多。 当然，考虑到我们正在用更有原则性的转变取代相对不系统的转变，我意识到这种变化不可能产生零影响，但总的来说，我们的绝大多数基准测试都没有看到性能变化。

最初，我们确实在许多程序中遇到了回归。 事实证明，其根源是不规则的嵌套并行性，旧的扁平化器会默默地将其视为顺序的，而将其视为顺序的确实是最佳策略。 作为示例，请考虑基准程序 hand.fut 中的以下函数：

def angle_axis_to_rotation_matrix (angle_axis: [3]f64) : [3][3]f64 =
  let n = f64.sqrt (angle_axis[0] ** 2 + angle_axis[1] ** 2 + angle_axis[2] ** 2)
  in if n < 0.0001
     then identity 3
     else let x = angle_axis[0] / n
          let y = angle_axis[1] / n
          let z = angle_axis[2] / n
          let s = f64.sin n
          let c = f64.cos n
          in [ [ x * x + (1 - x * x) * c
               , x * y * (1 - c) - z * s
               , x * z * (1 - c) + y * s
               ]
             , [ x * y * (1 - c) + z * s
               , y * y + (1 - y * y) * c
               , y * z * (1 - c) - x * s
               ]
             , [ x * z * (1 - c) - y * s
               , z * y * (1 - c) + x * s
               , z * z + (1 - z * z) * c
               ]
             ]

该函数在映射内部使用，并且由于条件 n < 0.0001 可能在映射的不同迭代之间变化，因此由于控制流，这是一个非均匀 if，尽管它生成的数组的大小是均匀的 [3][3]。 旧的扁平化器无法以任何特殊方式处理非均匀 if ，只是将整个事情转换为顺序代码，而新的扁平化器将应用裂变和 if 扁平化规则，以便利用 Identity 3 函数调用的并行性 - 它构造了一个 3x3 单位矩阵。 与展平 if 的簿记成本相比，这里的并行量完全不相关，因此这导致了性能的大幅下降。 增量扁平化并没有拯救我们，因为该函数是在同级代码包含重要并行性的上下文中使用的，并且增量扁平化在映射嵌套的每个级别都是全有或全无。

解决方案是向 if 添加 #[sequential] 属性，指示编译器应该将其顺序化。 我们已经在其他程序中使用此属性来指导沿着正确的路径进行增量扁平化，或者只是通过不生成不必要的版本来减少编译时间。 因此，虽然使用这样的属性并不优雅，但这意味着新的拼合器在做错事情时不需要全新的解决方法 - 旧的解决方法仍然可以使用。

遗憾的是，属性解决方案仅适用于用户可以看到的代码。 Futhark 还包含自动微分的复杂实现（真实的帖子尚未编写，但请参阅文档和这篇文章）。 当应用自动微分时，编译器会生成大量且相当复杂的代码，包括各种并行操作，但由于它不是由人类编写的代码，因此人类无法插入属性。 这意味着我们确实有一个程序（实际上又是 hand.fut），在雅可比行列式计算中，某些（不是全部）工作负载的速度减慢了 2 倍，因为伴随代码过度并行化。 另一方面，由于其伴随代码的额外并行化，相关基准 gmm.fut 在某些雅可比计算上出现了 4 倍的加速！ 我尝试了一下我们的启发法，看看是否可以想出一个简单的解决方案，但最终决定放弃它，直到我们更好地了解正确的解决方案是什么。 这意味着，一旦合并新的拼合器，某些程序的性能将会发生变化。

IR 不使用映射和扫描，而是具有专用结构，例如 segscan 和 segmap，它们可以表示多维常规分段操作。 由于该程序是不规则的，因此所有这些都是一维的（(gtid_7809 < m_7572)），并使用标志数组对结构进行编码。 程序首先通过调用内置函数builtin/segiota进行分段iota，然后执行分段扫描，最后提取每个段的最后一个元素。 请注意，builtin/segiota 不仅返回分段表示的数据和标志向量，还返回表示每个分段的起始偏移量的偏移向量。 这将在最终的 segmap 中使用。 一般来说，内置的不规则分段操作返回的信息多于最小的辅助信息，因为附加的数组通常是必要的，并且通常必须在内部进行计算。

未来

新的拼合器尚未合并，但很快就会合并。 唯一需要做的工作是总体简化和解决各种 TODO 注释 - 上面讨论的性能波动将留到将来。

在 NESL（和 DPH）中，展平用于支持不规则数组作为源语言中的编程构造。 在 Futhark 中，我们的目标更为温和：我们希望支持不规则嵌套并行性，但我们没有计划将不规则数组添加到源语言或 IR 中。 展平使用展平通道本身内部的定制表示来处理不规则的中间数组。 原则上我并不反对不规则数组，如果它们能够被有效地处理的话，但是如果我们添加它们，许多重要的 Futhark 功能（例如大小类型）和我们的 FFI 可能会变得更加复杂。 我更喜欢解决好小问题，而不是解决不好的大问题，而且解决 Futhark 相当小的设计所产生的问题已经花了好几年的时间——而且我们还没有完成。 我不太急于去寻找更大的问题。

也就是说，我确实认为我们可以以某种方式将扁平化作为一种​​编程结构，这将允许编写数据并行程序的新方法，特别是如果我们还允许递归的话。 到目前为止不允许递归的主要原因是我们没有在 GPU 上递归函数的编译策略，但扁平化变换现在会将递归移至 CPU，所以这个论点不再成立。 然而，这是未来一篇文章的主题——这篇文章已经足够长了。
